title: Birth, family and first hearing music in New Orleans
summary: La Rocca names his parents and siblings, his shoemaker father who played trumpet, riverfront and park music, and how at nine he took a cornet and taught himself tunes.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Now just tell the people who you are. This is the voice of Dominic James LaRocca, better known as Nick LaRocca, leader and manager of the world's first jazz band, known as the creators of jazz. I'll tell you about my early life in music and contact. I was born in 1889 in the city of New Orleans. My father's name was Geronimo LaRocca, who was a trumpet player like myself. My mother is Victoria D'Neena and out of that marriage came six children. I'll give you them in order. Rosario was the oldest. Antonia was my sister, was second. Maria was third. Bartholomew was four. I mean Dominic, Nick, that is me, was the fourth child. Bartholomew was the fifth child and Leonard was the sixth child. In my early life, the Italians or Germans and many people, they used to have birthday parties and different functions around the city. My father played in many bands about the city. And all he could get was free. He taught my sisters how to play. He taught my older brother how to play. And when it came to my turn, I was to become a doctor. He didn't want no music for me. But I craved music. And my early contact with music was out where my father would play like Spanish Ford or either the West End. And sometimes when he wasn't playing, he would take me out to White City and listen to the music. Or we'd go to the parks and listen to music. Or go on the river and listen to music. Because that was the main part of my father's trade. He was a shoe merchant. He sold shoes to the sailors and repaired them. And he spoke four different languages. My father lived, when he first opened his place at Washington Avenue in St. Thomas, he had a little shoe store and a shoe making place and repairing. And he made new shoes also. On a Sunday, when we weren't working, or my father wasn't working, he'd bring us out along the river, which was the Poor People's Promenade. At that time, they had no steamboats, steam ships. They had steamboats, but no steam ships. Ocean going that I seen. And the wharf was open to fail. And it was Poor People's Promenade. In the middle, they had boats that came from Portuguese. And each one of these boats had a band on them. Or sometimes a little accordion, or piccolo, or bass violin, or violin. The Italians were the same. They had a clarinet or piccolo with this accordion. It was a little bit octagon-shaped accordion that they played. And on Sundays, the Germans, I'm going ahead of my story. The Germans had all brass instruments. They had cornet, alto, baritone, and tuba. And they used a bass drum. And these men would go around the parts of the front part of the city, playing on the street corners, accepting gratuitous from the people with a hat. That was some of my musical education. And the more my father take me to these places, the more I was determined to play music. At the age of nine years old, I remember just as well as I am here today. I don't say that I have a better memory than anybody else. But we were going into Walwood, Spain. And they were just stringing the telephone wires and telegraph wires on St. Thomas Street, passing the street. They were putting up wires, telegraph wires. My uncle, Anthony Danina, had volunteered for the war to go to Spain. And all my mom, my dad and I was crying. So I stole this cornet and went down to the block and tried to learn this cornet. At first, I couldn't make no sounds out of it. I couldn't understand the way he would play it and play so easy with it. I was singing them out. I was blowing a note and another one. Then I got to playing bugle calls. Then we kids would go around the neighborhood way off from the house. And some would have wash bars, tin pans, and any old refuse kitchen utensil that they didn't use. Some had bricks, broomsticks, simulated soldiers. And they had an American flag, a little bit of piece of American flag that they had, because everybody had flags then. And they had a flag and they put it on a stick and it carried it. And down on Spain, we'd go all over the streets. We played a bugle call. That's all I knew. I later take in this cornet and I began to find all the notes what the keys was for. I took a piece of paper and the simple tunes that I knew like the chilling would sing. Here comes the boat around the bend. Goodbye my lover, goodbye. Loaded down with China men. Goodbye my lover, goodbye. Bye baby. such tunes like that and oh Uncle John da or I seen Washington cross the Delaware many tunes that children would sing around the corner ring around the rosy and the lining bridge is falling down those are the first tunes are committed to paper I took a piece of paper and I blow a note I put the name of the tune on the top and I'd mark whatever vowel correspond with the tone that I had in my my ear onto this paper and in about six months I was playing a few tunes I played won't you come home Bill Bailey I played who's that knocking that not knocking at the door some tune that boom boom you can't I can't remember the correct name but it's I think it has something to do with Bill Bailey won't you come over to my house that was one of
